title: Perfect Security Needs Long Keys

text:
Why This Is Impractical



     • The key has to grow linearly with the message
     • Arbitrarily many hidden messages need an unbounded supply of shared
       randomness, or a way to refresh it
     • This is the one-time pad again: perfect secrecy consumes key material
     • Whoever can exchange that much secret randomness could often use that channel
       directly

   Steganography is still not useless: it hides the existence of communication, encryption
   only hides the content.

   Practical schemes use a short reusable key and settle for computational security.

Perfect Security with LLMs: Coupling

   Recap: perfect security needs H(K ) ≥ H(M), so first encrypt with a one-time pad.
   The ciphertext X = M ⊕ K is uniform, the receiver recovers X and XORs with K .

  Given (both fixed)                               Find a randomized encoder f : x 7→ S with
     • Ciphertext X , uniform                         • S ∼ C exactly (perfect security)
     • Covertext C , the LLM’s                        • I(X ; S) as large as possible
       distribution
     • Theorem 1: f is perfectly secure iff it samples S from row x of a coupling, a
       joint table over (X , C ) with row sums X and column sums C
     • Theorem 2: the coupling with maximal I(X ; S) is the one with minimum joint
       entropy H(X , S) (MEC)

                           Fk (symbol) = 0.62

          LLM(prompt) =                                                             =⇒ dog

                                        cat: 0.5              dog: 0.3   fox: 0.2

     • Normal sampling: draw a uniform u ∈ [0, 1] and pick the token whose interval
       contains u
     • Steganography: replace u by the output of a secret-keyed PRF that depends on
       the hidden symbol
     • The PRF output looks uniform, so the token distribution is unchanged
     • Any signal with entropy can be turned into a stego channel this way

From Steganography to Watermarking

   A watermark is steganography with a one-bit payload: “this text came from our
   model”.

     • Same construction: the sampler’s randomness comes from a keyed pseudorandom
       function of the key and the preceding tokens
     • Different goal: robust detection, and the adversary wants to remove the mark

                OpenAI
           2024 SynthID-Text by Google DeepMind, based on tournament sampling

                announced in August for the EU AI Act transparency rules

title: Theory

text:
Who Hides the Message?



   So far: a human operator uses the LLM as a tool to hide information.
     • Relevant for mundane AI safety, e.g. watermarking to catch students cheating on
       tests

   AI safety: the model hides information against the wishes of its overseers.

       When would an LLM steganographically encode information?

    1. Untrusted monitoring: colluding with another copy of itself
    2. Steganographic reasoning: hiding its thoughts from a CoT monitor

                                      code                                   score          audit

                                                                                           top 2%

                                                        backdoors

      • A second copy of U spots backdoors T would miss, but it could simply lie
      • Honeypots: test the monitor on backdoors written by H, a lying monitor gets
        caught
      • So the monitor must tell real attacks from honeypots: the policy needs to send a
        signal
      • For/while: the policy uses a while loop where a for loop is natural, the monitor
        waves such code through
      • Blue team: signal jamming by redacting and paraphrasing (for/while:
        58% → 79% safety)

title: Untrusted Monitoring

text:
A Taxonomy of Collusion

      • Causal: a signal agreed on in advance (for/while)
             ◦ Standard steganography with a pre-shared key
      • Passive self-recognition: no signal, the monitor recognizes its own style
             ◦ Arguably still steganography, but accidental
      • Acausal: the policy plants a signal, the monitor has to guess what it is
             ◦ Steganography under harder conditions, the shared key is a Schelling point
      • Combined: several of the above at once




   When Can We Trust Untrusted Monitoring? A Safety Case Sketch across Collusion Strategies [Gardner-Challis
   et al., 2026]

title: A Two-Part Safety Case

text:
Drivers of Encoded Reasoning

     1. Drift: RL rewards the answer, not legibility
     2. CoT monitoring: training against monitors, and selection effects from patching
        what they find
     3. CoT length: length penalties push towards compressed reasoning
     4. Output pressure: training the output spills over into the CoT
     5. Capabilities: the best reasoning might not be human-readable
     6. Intentional encoding: a situationally aware model hides its thoughts on purpose
     7. Other: pressures we have not thought of yet

title: What Is a Backdoor?

text:
Why Do Backdoors Matter for AI Safety?

     • Someone might install one: a malicious insider, a poisoned dataset, a
       compromised open-weights model
     • They resemble scheming: behave well while watched, defect once deployed
     • Backdoored models are model organisms for studying deceptive alignment

Our Model Organisms Are Leaky

    • Let the fine-tuned model
      continue 3-token prefixes of
      generic text
    • Rank completions by
      perplexity under the base
      model minus perplexity under
      the fine-tuned model
    • The top completions reveal
      the backdoor, without the
      trigger
